title: The True Story Behind Flags Of Our Fathers: The Two Flags Of Iwo Jima

beats.text: It is the most famous photograph of the Second World War. Six men pushing a flag pole into the sky on top of a volcano.

v.q: Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima

beats.text: But it was not the first flag. Another flag had already been flying on that mountain for about two hours.

v.q: First flag raising Iwo Jima Lowery

beats.text: And for seventy four years, the United States Marine Corps had the names of the men in the picture wrong.

v.q: Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima

beats.text: The film Flags of Our Fathers told part of this story. The real story is stranger, and a lot sadder.
Iwo Jima is a tiny island in the Pacific, about seven hundred and fifty miles south of Tokyo. It is only about eight square miles.
It had almost no water, no trees and no towns worth taking. What it had was airfields.
American bombers flying from the Mariana Islands to Japan passed right over it. Japanese fighters and radar on Iwo Jima warned the mainland and attacked the bombers.
If America took the island, damaged bombers would have a place to land halfway home.
At the southern tip stood a dead volcano, Mount Suribachi, about five hundred and fifty feet high. From the top, you could see the whole island.
The Japanese commander, General Tadamichi Kuribayashi, knew he could not win. So he planned to make the battle as costly as possible.
He did not defend the beaches. He put his roughly twenty thousand men underground.
They dug miles of tunnels, caves and bunkers through the soft volcanic rock, and they were ordered to kill ten Americans each before they died.
For months American planes bombed the island, and for three days before the landing the navy shelled it. Most of the defenders simply waited below.
On the nineteenth of February 1945, the Marines landed.
The black volcanic sand was so soft that men sank to their ankles and vehicles got stuck on the beach.
Then, once the beach was crowded, the hidden guns opened fire.
By the end of the first day, about thirty thousand Marines were ashore, and more than two thousand of them were dead or wounded.
The first job was to cut off Suribachi. The 28th Marine Regiment fought its way across the narrow neck of the island and then turned toward the mountain.
For four days they attacked its slopes, cave by cave.
On the morning of the twenty third of February, a patrol of about forty men from Easy Company was sent up to the summit.
They were led by First Lieutenant Harold Schrier. In his pack was a small American flag, taken from a navy transport ship.
They expected a fight at the top. Instead it was quiet.
The men found a length of iron pipe, tied the flag to it, and pushed it into the ground on the rim of the crater.

v.q: First flag raising Iwo Jima Lowery

beats.text: A Marine photographer, Sergeant Louis Lowery, took pictures of the moment.
Down on the beaches, men saw the tiny flag. They cheered. Ships offshore blew their horns.
Then Japanese soldiers came out of a cave and attacked the patrol. Lowery dove away and broke his camera, but his film survived.
On the beach, the Secretary of the Navy, James Forrestal, had just come ashore.
He turned to the Marine general Holland Smith and said this.
The raising of that flag on Suribachi means a Marine Corps for the next five hundred years.

v.text: The raising of that flag on Suribachi means a Marine Corps for the next 500 years.

beats.text: And then Forrestal said he wanted that flag as a souvenir.
The battalion commander, Lieutenant Colonel Chandler Johnson, did not like that at all. The flag belonged to his men.
So, the story goes, he ordered a second, bigger flag to be taken up the mountain, so the first one could come down and stay with the battalion.
The bigger flag, about eight feet long, came from a landing ship on the beach.
A young runner named Rene Gagnon carried it up the slope, along with fresh radio batteries.
With him went a small team led by Sergeant Michael Strank, who had been sent up to lay a telephone wire.
Behind them, three combat photographers were climbing too. One of them was Joe Rosenthal of the Associated Press.
Rosenthal almost did not go up. On the way, he met Lowery coming down, who told him the flag was already raised.
He climbed anyway, because the view from the top might still make a good picture.
At the top, Rosenthal saw a group of Marines tying the big flag to a heavy pipe. The old flag was about to come down.
He was short, so he piled up some stones and sandbags to stand on.
Right next to him, Marine Sergeant Bill Genaust was holding a movie camera loaded with colour film.
Out of the corner of his eye Rosenthal saw the pole start to rise. He swung his camera up and pressed the button without looking through the viewfinder properly.

v.q: Iwo Jima flag raising film Genaust

beats.text: It took a fraction of a second. He had no idea if he had even caught it.

v.q: Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima

beats.text: Then, to be safe, he asked a group of Marines to gather and wave under the flag. He called it his gung-ho shot.

v.q: Gung Ho photo Iwo Jima Rosenthal

beats.text: That second picture would cause him trouble for the rest of his life.
His film was flown to Guam to be developed. When the editor saw the flag picture, he knew at once what it was.
Within about two days it was on the front pages of newspapers all over America.
Weeks later a journalist asked Rosenthal if the photo was posed. He thought they meant the gung-ho group shot, and said sure.

v.by: Joe Rosenthal, asked if it was posed

beats.text: A rumour started that the famous flag raising was staged. Rosenthal spent decades denying it.

v.q: Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima

beats.text: The proof was in Genaust's colour film, which shows the flag going up from almost the same spot, in one real movement.

v.q: Iwo Jima flag raising film Genaust

beats.text: Genaust never got to defend his own film. About ten days later he was killed in a cave on the island. His body was never found.
Back home, the photo became a symbol overnight, and the president wanted the men in it sent home.
The government wanted them for a war bond tour. America needed money to finish the war.
But there was a problem. In the photo you cannot see a single face clearly. So who were they?

v.q: Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima

beats.text: By then, some of them were already dead.
Sergeant Michael Strank and Corporal Harlon Block were killed on the first of March. Private Franklin Sousley was killed three weeks later.
Rene Gagnon was asked to name the men. He named Harlon Block's place in the photo as Henry Hansen, a man who was actually in the first flag raising.
Harlon Block's mother looked at the picture and said that was her son. Almost nobody listened to her.
It was Ira Hayes, a Pima Marine from Arizona, who finally backed her up. In 1947 the Marine Corps corrected the record.
Three of the men were sent on the bond tour: Gagnon, Hayes, and a navy medic named John Bradley.

v.q: Ira Hayes Rene Gagnon John Bradley 1945

beats.text: The Seventh War Loan raised more than twenty six billion dollars.
Ira Hayes hated being called a hero while his friends lay buried on the island. He struggled with drinking, and he died in 1955 at just thirty two.
John Bradley went home, became a funeral director, and almost never talked about it.
After he died, his son James wrote the book Flags of Our Fathers. Clint Eastwood turned it into the film.
And here is the twist. Years after the film, amateur historians studied the photos frame by frame, and spotted something.

v.q: Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima

beats.text: The man everyone thought was John Bradley was wearing different gear from what Bradley wore that day.

v.q: Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima detail

beats.text: In 2016 the Marine Corps agreed. John Bradley was in the first flag raising, but not in the famous photo. The man was Private Harold Schultz.
Schultz almost never spoke about it, and he died in 1995 without ever going public.
Then in 2019 came a second correction. Rene Gagnon, the runner who carried the flag up the mountain, is not in the photo either. The man was Corporal Harold Keller.
So the man who brought the famous flag to the top was not in the famous picture, and he spent his life on stage as one of its heroes.
Today the six men are listed as Strank, Block, Sousley, Hayes, Schultz and Keller.

v.title: THE SIX MEN, AS NOW LISTED

v.q: Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima

beats.text: And the battle? When the second flag went up, it was only day five. The fighting went on for more than a month.
Almost seven thousand Americans were killed. Of the roughly twenty thousand Japanese defenders, only a few hundred were taken alive.

v.title: THE COST
lines: only a few hundred Japanese captured

beats.text: It was one of the very few Pacific battles where American casualties were higher than Japanese ones.
Twenty seven Medals of Honor were awarded for Iwo Jima, one of the highest numbers for any single battle in American history.
General Kuribayashi died in the last days of the fighting. His body was never identified.
And the damaged bombers did use the island. Thousands of crewmen landed safely on Iwo Jima before the war ended.
Both flags survive. They hang today in the National Museum of the Marine Corps in Virginia.

v.q: National Museum of the Marine Corps

beats.text: So how true is the famous version? The flag raising was real. It was not staged.

v.q: Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima

beats.text: But it was the second flag, raised by a mix of men no one could name for seventy four years, and three of them never came home.

v.q: Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima
